qs.q: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) typically originates in which zone of the prostate gland?
qs.e: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) predominantly develops in the transition zone of the prostate, which surrounds the urethra. Prostate cancer typically originates in the peripheral zone.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is an age‑related, androgen‑driven growth of prostate tissue that narrows the urethra, causing urinary symptoms. Diagnosis relies on history, digital rectal exam, PSA, and imaging when needed. Management balances symptom relief, medication choice, and monitoring for complications.

sections.p: BPH is a non‑cancerous proliferation of stromal and glandular cells in the transitional zone, driven by dihydrotestosterone. It is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by prostate volume and PSA trends.
b: Digital rectal exam (DRE) shows a firm, nodular prostate

t.b: Is PSA elevated in BPH? PSA rises with prostate size; a value >4 ng/mL warrants further workup for cancer.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and prostate volume. Staging guides treatment intensity.

t.b: Quantifies symptom burden; higher scores predict need for medication or surgery.

sections.p: The primary driver is androgen excess, especially DHT, acting on androgen receptors in prostatic cells. Secondary factors include aging, inflammation, and comorbidities.

t.b: Increased activity leads to higher DHT; explains why 5α‑reductase inhibitors work.
Elevated CRP or ESR may suggest prostatitis contributing to symptoms.

faq.a: No, BPH is benign; however, both share risk factors and PSA can be elevated in either.
